messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 54
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Community Organizer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Darkness: Dark spaces, Spatial Triggers: Physical locations, Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people, Avoid Event Site: avoid site of the event, Concealing Clothing: wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
  Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted, Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am, Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ahmed is a 54-year-old Middle Eastern man who has been coming to therapy after experiencing significant distress following prolonged physical abuse from his romantic partner. He lives in a community where he serves as a dedicated and passionate community organizer. His journey began several years ago when he entered into what he initially believed was a loving relationship, only to find himself trapped in an abusive situation. The traumatic events were not isolated incidents but rather a series of violent episodes that occurred over months, each one escalating in intensity. Ahmed vividly remembers the darkened rooms and small spaces where his partner would isolate him, leaving him feeling both physically and emotionally suffocated. The sounds of helicopters flying overhead during those times added to the terror, as he was often taken to remote locations for these episodes. Since then, Ahmed has found himself hyper-vigilant around people, constantly scanning the environment for signs of danger or betrayal. This hypervigilance is especially pronounced in dark spaces and at certain physical locations that remind him of the abuse. As a result, he avoids those places entirely, which has impacted his ability to move freely within his community. In an effort to maintain anonymity and reduce his visibility, Ahmed often wears concealing clothing to avoid being noticed by others who might trigger memories of the abuse. His hypervigilance extends to auditory cues as well; any sound resembling a helicopter instantly plunges him back into those terrifying moments, leaving him feeling helpless and exposed. His memory of these events is fragmented and disjointed, with pieces that do not fit together. When triggered by sounds or locations, he sometimes hears the voices and noises from those traumatic episodes playing in his head, as if they were happening all over again. This has made it incredibly difficult for him to function normally without being overcome by flashbacks and intense distress. Ahmed harbors deep feelings of betrayal, believing that someone he trusted could hurt him so severely. He also questions the kind of person he must be for such an event to have happened to him, leading to a profound sense of character blame. These beliefs are intertwined with shattered trust in the world around him, making it hard for him to find solace or security even in his everyday surroundings. As a community organizer, Ahmed’s work has been profoundly affected by these struggles. He avoids certain parts of the city where he used to organize events and meetings, leading to strained relationships with colleagues who do not understand why he is no longer as involved. This avoidance has also led to reduced productivity at work and a sense of isolation from his professional community. The culmination of these experiences finally brought Ahmed to seek help when he realized that he was unable to maintain his role in the community without compromising his own mental health. He is most afraid of being trapped again, either by circumstances or by the memories that haunt him, but he also harbors a glimmer of hope for reclaiming his life and finding peace within himself. In therapy, Ahmed hopes to regain some sense of control over his life and work through the lingering trauma so that he can return to the community organizer role he loves, free from the constant fear and distress. His journey is one of resilience and determination in the face of overwhelming adversity, seeking a path back to trust and healing.
